Lobster season changed from April 26 to May 4; unsatisfactory to majority fishermen and packers. Please ascertain on what grounds and representations this change was made. Cumberland county inspector or packers not consulted.

speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext: The change has been agreed upon as a result of numerous representations to the effect that on account of ice conditions it was impracticable to start the fishing season on the 26th, which is the normal date for the opening of that season in this particular district. Representations have been made to the department and to myself personally bymembers of this House, as well as by telegrams and letters from interested parties. All the representations were based upon the ice conditions in this part of the country, but in the meantime we have received word that the ice is gone and that conditions now permit the opening of the season. Accordingly we issued orders this morning that the opening of the season should not be delayed any longer, and that fishing can be commenced this morning.

speechtext: May I ask the Secretary of State whether he is now able to give a further reply to my question of Friday last regarding the oil companies of the province of Alberta, the charters of which have been withheld, and as to whether the oil companies to which he promised charters have as yet received them?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Referring to the second question I have given instructions that these charters should be sent to the parties applying for them, and I have no doubt they have been forwarded. In reference to the next part of this question, I have prepared a statement which I desire to read:
Until quite recently applications for the incorporation of local mining and oil ccmpau.es have not been made under the Dominion Companies Act. It is the practice of the Department of the Secretary of State not to incorporate companies having local activities only. Such companies are within the jurisdiction of the provinces. The Dominion, however, incorporates companies where it is stated in the applications that the operations will be carried on in more than one province.
The recent oil development ;n the province of Alberta has been the occasion of a large number of applications for the incorporation of oil companies. In each case it has been alleged by the applicants that they propose carrying on business in more than one province. It is impossible to investigate the genuineness of intentions, and tile department has been forced to accept these statements.
It is suggested, however, that ihe reason for these applications being made to the Department of the Secretary of State, is the decision of the Supreme court in Ihe case of Lukey versus The Rutiienian Farmers' Elevator Company, in which it was held that Dominion companies are not subject to the Sale of Shares Acts of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. If this allegation is well founded, the immediate inference is that many of these companies are what is generally known as "wild cats", brought
Fraudulent Companies

into existence for the purpose of selling shares rather than boring for oil. The fact that Dominion oil company charters are advertised in the Calgary press, indicates a very unsatisfactory condition.
The western provinces are agitating for an amendment to the Dominion Companies Act under wh'ch Dominion companies would be made subject to the Sale of Shares Acts of these provinces. This is a difficult question and it raises many others which should be discussed when the necessary amendment of the Companies Act is under consideration. For that reason such an amendment could not be submitted to parliament at the present session and could not likely be dealt with until the next session of parliament. By then the deluge of oil company flotations may be over, and in the meantime it is necessary to take some action to protect the investing public.
It is a widely-held belief that the voluntary provision of the Companies Act, under which shares without nominal or par value are issued, are more effective in protecting the public than "blue sky" legislation. This was one of the principal arguments put forward when these provisions were adopted. It has been decided, therefore, that in applications for the incorporation of oil and mining companies, which are suspected to be purely local concerns, the charter shall limit the issue of shares to shares without nominal or par value.

May I ask the Secretary of
State if that regulation is to be made retroactive?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It will not be retroactive concerning those companies mentioned by my hon. friend, to whom assurances have been given that charters will be issued, but for other companies it will be retroactive.

speechtext:
The House resumed from Tuesday, April 27, the debate on the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Hon. R. J. Manion.
Mr. ROBERT IC. SMITH (Cumberland): Mr. Speaker, with the permission and indulgence of the House, I intend to make some observations on the budget in its particular application to some of the many interests in the eastern portion of the Dominion of Canada and the Maritime provinces. The House has been treated, if I. may be permitted to use the phrase in that sense, to many matters of concern directly affecting us in the east, and what I shall have to say will not be in any sense a survey of our Maritime situation or a review of the seriousness of the difficulties under which we are labouring, which have already been quite fully stated, or of the grave burdens which we are forced to bear under ordinary circumstances without relation to the customs tariff.
It will be recognized at once that many of our troubles and difficulties have a close bearing on the tariff-coal, steel, agriculture, and our industries, for instance- while other problems apparently difficult of solution, such as transportation, have no bearing on the tariff. It is with the former-coal, steel, agriculture and industrial pursuits, or certain phases of them-that I desire to place some facts before this hon. House, and it will be observed that the remarks I have to offer apply not alone to the Maritime provinces, but to other portions of Canada, in fact, to the whole Dominion.
My first, word, Mr. Speaker, on the budget as brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is that it is a notable one, notable I believe mainly for its omissions and its startling disregard for some of the main interests of this country, most particular'/
the labouring class. It is my purpose to place before the House some of the very striking omissions affecting materially, in my opinion, the portion of Canada from which I come, and having a general effect throughout the country through lack of recognition in a protective manner.
We from Nova Scotia have stressed the urgent need and long overdue protection essential to our two main industries, coal and steel. This government in its frantic desire to cater entirely to the western portion of Canada has entirely overlooked our legitimate and reasonable request for protection on these two main key industries. This request has been treated with somewhat of a silent and unwarranted contempt. I presume that some members may think that our mouths from the Maritime provinces should be closed because a royal commission has been appointed to investigate Maritime conditions. Whatever may be thought in this connection, I wish to make perfectly clear to the House that I do not intend to surrender my constitutional privilege, yes, my bounden duty to represent as best I can my riding by placing before parliament the views of the people who sent me here, royal commission or no royal commission. I trust that the royal commission appointed will serve some good purpose in the province of Nova Scotia after they have reviewed our distressing situation, but whether they do so or not, it is not my intention to forfeit what I consider to be my plain duty to the riding which sent me here, and that is to place the situation and circumstances affecting us as I see them before the House, and to offer whatever suggestions I can in my humble way to remedy the present conditions.
Much has been said, Mr. Speaker, on both sides of the House for and against this budget, appertaining to the changes, forecasts and their effects. It will be my humble task to deal as best I can with matters entirely overlooked by the Minister of Finance, some of which, and one in particular, have been brought very pertinently before this House during this session, but have been entirely disregarded by this government of lower tariffs and many diversified elements. I refer particularly to the question of coal.
First let me repeat what I stated in this connection in the House some weeks ago, that the frantic demand for increased duty on coal was brought to a head in Nova Scotia in December, 1924, when Liberals, Conservatives, and all others united and sent a delegation to Ottawa demanding more duty on coal and steel. That delegation was headed by the Hon. E. H. Armstrong, who was at that time
The Budget-Mr. Smith

Liberal premier of the province of Nova Scotia, and with the permission of the House I should like to quote some of the appeals made by the delegation through their spokesman, ex-Premier Armstrong, to the government on that occasion. These appeals are tersely stated, being extracts from the memorandum which was presented to the government by the delegation on that occasion. I quote:
"The allied coal and steel industries of Nova Scotia have been for some years in a depressed condition."
"The prospect for the future is that there may be even more serious depression and resultant poverty."
"The Province of Nova Scotia is largely dependent upon these industries which are the main, and in some instances, the sole support of the population in important centres."
"This will be easily understood when it is considered that from 20.000 to 25,000 men are employed in the mining of coal and its associated industries."
"And that directly dependent on these there are not less than 100,000 to 125,000 people, or more than ore-fifth of the population of the Province."
The delegation asked the King government for adequate tariff protection to prevent foreign coal and steel products from flooding Canada's markets:	to
stabilize and promote the coal and steel industries in Nova Scotia; and give the workingmen engaged in them steady and remunerative employment.
That delegation was splendidly received by the government. Their appeals were taken into consideration by the Prime Minister and his government, and the result was that when the budget was brought down in 1925 it contained an increase in the duty on slack coal from 14 cents to 50 cents a ton, and a decrease in the duties on screened and run-of-mine coal from 53 cents to 50 cents a ton. This change did not produce the favourable results that were desired in connection with the coal industry of the province of Nova Scotia. Now, I call attention to the fact that in this House a few days ago, speaking about the increases last year in the duty on slack coal, the Prime Minister stated that this was a case where relief was necessary and where the exception proved the rule; that it was a good thing to give our slack coal more protection, and he urged his Progressive friends to support the exception. If it was necessary to make an exception then I ask why not make an exception noV? The conditions are worse now than they were then. Therefore, why not follow the exception to its logical conclusion, and give the industry the protection it requires? The Prime Minister realized the necessity and admitted the urgency of more protection on slack coal. He is quoted as having said that no legitimate industry in Canada Would suffer from the fiscal policy of his government. This industry is suffering, has been suffering, and will continue to suffer until it is relieved by

adequate protection. It is suffering under the fiscal policy of the present government, and we would like to take the Prime Minister at his word in this matter. I might refer to the fact that some of his candidates in Nova Scotia in the campaign of 1925 advocated higher duty on coal and steel.
For the information of the House I will review the duties on coal in Canada from 1867 to date. From December 21, 1867, to May 12, 1870, coal and coke were free. From May 12, 1870 to April 1, 1871, there was a duty of 50 cents per ton on coal and coke. From April 1, 1871 to March 15, 1879, coal and coke were free again. From March 15, 1879, to May 7, 1880, there was a duty of 50 cents per ton on coal and coke. From May 7, 1880, to April 20, 1883 there was a duty of 50 cents per ton on anthracite coal, a duty of 60 cents per ton on bituminous coal, and a duty of 50 cents per ton on coke. From April 20, 1883, to May 13, 1887, there was a duty of 50 cents per ton on anthracite coal, a duty of 60 cents per ton on bituminous coal, a duty of 20 per cent on bituminous coal dust, and a duty of 50 cents per ton on coke. From May 13, 1887, to March 28, 1890, anthracite was free. There was a duty of 60 cents per ton on bituminous coal, a duty of 20 per cent on bituminous coal dust, and a duty of 50 cents per ton on coke. From March 28, 1890, to March 27, 1891, anthracite coal and anthracite coal dust were free. There was a duty of 60 cents per ton on bituminous coal, a duty of 20 per cent on bituminous coal dust, gas coke for Canadian manufacturers was free, and there was a duty of 50 cents per ton on coke. From March 27, 1891, to April 23, 1S97, there was no duty on anthracite coal or anthracite coal dust. On bituminous coal there was a duty of 60 cents per ton, a duty of 20 per cent on bituminous coal dust, and coke was on the free list. From April 23, 1897, to November 30, 1906, anthracite coal and anthracite coal dust were on the free list. Cn bituminous slack coal such as would pass through a half-inch screen, there was a duty of 20 per cent. On bituminous coal -round and run-of-mine-there was a duty of 53 cents per ton, and coke was on the free list. From November 30, 1906, to March 25, 1925, there was no duty on anthracite coal or anthracite coal dust. On bituminous slack coal there was a duty of 14 cents per ton. On bituminous coal-round and run-of-mine- there was a duty of 53 cents -per ton. From March 25, 1925 to date, anthracite coal and anthracite coal dust are on the free list. There is a duty of 50 cents per ton on bituminous coal and coal not otherwise provided for. Coke is placed on the free list.

The Budget-Mr. Smith
It will be noted that in the placing of the duties, from April, 1867, down to date, there has not been a very great spread in the amount of duty on the product of coal; the duty has ranged around 50 cents per ton ever since it was first placed. It will be recognized at once, I think, by every reasonable person that if 50 cents per ton was adequate protection back in the seventies it is surely not adequate protection to-day. The increased cost in the price of coal is so apparent and so evident, and is felt to such an extent by every manufacturer and householder in this Dominion, as to obviate any necessity of labouring that particular argument. As a matter of fact we have not one-half the protection on coal to-day that we had back in the seventies on account of the increase in the price of the product; and in Nova Scotia we are urging that this particular point be taken into consideration by the government and that it be regulated in accordance with the price of coal to-day.
It has been stated that in order to have more of our own coal used, a campaign of education should be carried on in this country. This may be so, but if there is to be a campaign of education there must also be one of example. The largest publicly owned corporation in Canada that I know of is the Canadian National Railway. I should like to ask the House what example it sets with regard to the use of Canadian coal on the National system of railways. The importations of coal into Canada for the past ten years show an average of over 15,000,000 tons per annum. This is most significant, in view of the fact that there has been stagnation of a very startling character in the coal mining districts in the Dominion of Canada. As I stated, our coal miners are not able to procure work. They are not able properly to feed and clothe their families, but at the same time we are importing from a foreign country over 15,000,000 tons of coal annually. Think of an industry in Canada being exploited, our miners thrown out of employment and our coal provinces commercially stagnated, not to mention the Canadian money, over a hundred million dollars, being spent for the purchase of American coal, providing employment for American miners to the detriment of our own miners, and incidentally increasing the wealth of the United States, at the same time reducing our own wealth in Canada, and allowing our Canadian market for coal to be robbed by American operators. If we follow this suicidal policy in other things, I think it will be found before long that, as a business country, we will have to pull down the blinds, nail up the shutters, lock the door and disappear. Our coal resources in Canada are of a very substantial character. Our consumption of coal in Canada annually is nearly 29,000,000 tons. Cur own Canadian coal supplies only 12,000,000 of that market, approximately 17,000,000 tons being supplied by foreign countries, and still we have no relief from this government in this connection. Let me quote the importations in 1925 into this country. They are as follows:

Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not feel that it is necessary to deal with those figures which are accurate, being government figures, and which speak very loudly in regard to the great disadvantage the coal miners all over the Dominion of Canada are labouring under on account of being robbed of the Canadian market which is going to a foreign country and, as I said before, being exploited by foreign mine operators. Let me examine for a minute the policy of the leader of the government in Canada in connection with the coal mining industry. I am quoting from a Canadian press report of an address of the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister of Canada, delivered at Orillia, Ontario, October 15, 1925, and I find the following:
As at Parry Sound, Mr. . King attacked Mr. Meighen's proposal to put a tariff on foreign coal, and to give assistance out of federal taxes to transportation rates from Maritimes and the west to the central provinces. "I do not think/' said Mr. King, "that the people fully realize what this proposal means. At a moment when the nation is striving to throw off the burden of taxation Mr. Meighen is proposing to add to the burden of taxation. I have seen some winters in Canada when we have almost had to go down on our knees for the coal needed in the homes and factories of this country."
I think that the policy as outlined by the Prime Minister at Orillia last October is a policy, if followed, so far as we are concerned in the eastern portions of the Dominion of Canada, will ruin our coal and steel industries completely and entirely, and the importance of this industry in our province I think may be gauged from the fact that one-fifth of the entire population is wholly dependent on it.
Then, Mr. Speaker, in this connection I wish to deal with the source of supply today from the American coal mines. I think this applies particularly to the anthracite coal mines in the United States of America. The supply is not inexhaustible. It is estimated, an.l I think it was mentioned by the hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Macdougall) in this House not long ago, that twenty-five years at the outside will exhaust the supply of anthracite coal from the United States. So that we in Canada, whether we desire it or not, will be driven to the use of our own coal after that period and perhaps before. If we must in the end be driven to the use of our own Canadian coal, why not adopt that policy now? Why not build up our own Canadian market for our own Canadian, miners, and then when the time comes we will be ready for any exigency on account of the exhaustion of the supply in other-countries?
I think it might very reasonably be expected tha* if double the present supply of the Canadian coal were granted to the Canadian miners in the future, if they could secure double the market in Canada that they have to-day, there would be a material decrease in the price of coal. I am positively sure that if there was a market for Nova Scotia coal double the market of to-day, it could be reasonably expected that there would be a substantial decrease in the cost
The Budget-Mr. Smith

of coal to the consumer. It seems to me that if it could be guaranteed to our Canadian mine operators that we would receive approximately 20,000,000 tons of the 29,000.000 tons consumed, we might have every reason to hope for a reduction in the price, and if we were to place, as we must place in order to protect this industry, a duty of $1 a ton on coal, it would not mean that the consumer would have to pay more for his coal, because the increased production and the volume would more than offset any other disadvantages in this connection. I think it is reasonable to argue, Mr. Speaker, that this industry would prove to be one of very great importance to Canada, much more so than it is to-day, and the Canadian consumer would also be almost guaranteed a reduction in the price of coal
I desire to quote from the report of the Royal Coai Commission investigating this matter in Nova Scotia last year. The reason I do so is that in the addendum to the main report, which was presented by Major Hume Cronyn, the coal situation is dealt with in very terse language. In the addendum Major Hume Cronyn says:
As a native and resident of the one, and a life-long admirer of the other, I take the liberty of making this appeal on behalf not only of Nova Scotia, but indeed of the well-being of the Dominion as a whole.
It will appeal from our report that one, perhaps the greatest, cause of distress and discontent is due to irregularity of employment in the mines. At the moment this statement is being penned there have been further outbreaks of violence in Cape Breton due to lack of employment with the destitution and ill-feeling consequent thereon.
The reasons for unemployment have already been explained, but to my mind that one which overshadows all others is -the inability of Nova Scotia coals to compete in the St. Lawrence markets with those imported from the United States. This condition is due to the fact that in certain of the American coal fields, notably those of West Virginia, coal can be produced at a much lower cost than is possible in eastern Canada. Some of the factors explanatory of this lower cost may be briefly set out:
(1)	-The ease with which coal can be mined and conveyed to the pit mouth.
(2)	-The absence of gas and the benefit accruing from natural drainage.
(3)	-The many economies possible, due to the fact that submarine mining in unknown, whereas more than half the output in Nova Scotia is mined several miles under the sea.
The marked difference in mining costs due to the above causes enables American coals to be transported, largely by water, from the field named and, after payment of the present Canadian import duty of 50 cents per ton, to be sold in Montreal and other Canadian -markets at prices below the actual cost of production and transportation of Nova Scotia coal.
Most of the remedies suggested and set out below were forcibly brought to the attention of the Dominion government in December, 1924, by a representative delegation headed by the then premier of Nova Scotia. It would be a lengthy and perhaps unprofitable task to examine in detail the merits of each; suffice it to
[Mr. Smith.)	-
say that in my opinion the two first named are those best fitted to bring relief to what is little less than a national calamity.
1st.-Federal assistance towards the establishment of coking ovens. This remedy has been fully discussed in section 36 of our report and need not be further elaborated.
2nd.-A substantial increase in the import duty on all bituminous coal and anthracite screenings; or, in the alternative, a federal bounty on coal shipped from the Maritimes to Montreal or beyond, and on coal shipped from Alberta or British Columbia to Winnipeg or eastward.
Further on Mr. Cronyn states:
The economist may logically ask why an industry which cannot survive competition should be allowed to exist and consumers in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario may denounce any increase in the tariff as that must inevitably raise the price of bituminous coal. As one whose academic ifcrainiing -has been that of the Manchester school I must admit the cogency of both question and denunciation. But there are considerations involved in this problem which transcend cold-blooded political economy or even the losses which may fall on the more thickly settled portions of Canada.
May I attempt in the briefest fashion to outline these considerations.
More than one-fifth of the population of the province of Nova Scotia are directly dependent upon its coal industries and the subsidiaries thereof and over 12 per cent of the revenues of the province are derived from the royalties -paid on coal mined. After spending weeks on the ground and discussing the question with many residents of the province -in all walks of life I concur in the statement made by -the deputation before mentioned that "It is not possible to exaggerate the calamitous consequences to Canada should coal mining in Nova Scotia be permitted ,to decline."
Let us consider -but two of these consequences. We in Ontario are accustomed, if not hardened, to the accusation made in the prairie provinces that -the east treats the west unfaiMy but the sense of grievances unredressed which prompts -this charge is as nothing to the depth of feeling which exists in the Maritimes against the central provinces of Ontario and Quebec. That resentment is of old standing and one of its causes is the belief that the Atlantic provinces were more or less cajoled into confederation by promises and alluring prospects which have failed of fulfilment. It is indeed not going too far to say that the tie of sentiment which binds Nova Scotia to the Dominion has worn very thin.
If then we of the central provinces are unwilling to sacrifice something of our prosperity on the altar of common citizenship to aid, perhaps indeed to save, the main industry of Nova Scotia, we may witness an estrangement of far reaching consequences. For it is not exaggerating the situation to say that the inhabitants of the Maritime provinces are in a frame of mind that insists upon relief from the disadvantages under which they labour.
Then he goes on to state:
My appeal then to my friends (if I may so term them) of Quebec and Ontario and through them to the parliament of Canada is on the highest ground of national unity. Let us, overlooking the pecuniary sacrifices invoked, take the necessary measures to safeguard the welfare of our brothers by th'e sea.
The second calamitous consequence to central Canada which might follow a collapse of coal miming in Nova Scotia will become clear if we but exercise sufficient foresight to discover what will be the probable course of events in regard to the supply of American anthracite upon which to-day we almost wholly depend for

The Budget-Mr. Smith
domestic heating. As our reports sets forth the lifetime of the mines from which we are supplied is limited and -their exhaustion is already in sight. At the same time -the demand for the American market has enormously increased. In the Light of former aotions, political and otherwise, and bearing in mind the warnings already given us, we need not be surprised if at some not far distant future an embargo be placed upon the export of anthracite. Should we not then be forehanded enough to protect ourselves against this day of reckoning by so encouraging the development of a native -industry as to have avaiilo-b-le a plentiful supply of that unexcelled substitute, to wit: Canadian coke?
Lest objection be taken that from one cause or another Nova Scotia might be unable to supply the coal or coke necessary for our requirements it is suggested that the increase of the customs tariff or bounty grants should only remain in force so long as it is clear that the supply of the native product is ample for all purposes.
The reason I read that quotation at some length was because of what I consider the very sound commonsense displayed therein.
We want only sufficient protection 4 p.m. on our coal to protect the industry in order to protect the Canadian market for our Canadian coal miners. If a dollar a ton duty will serve that end, well and good; if seventy-five cents a ton duty will serve it, all right. We have no objection; we are not making a particular plea, stating any positive and specific amount of duty that should be imposed, but we ask that a sufficient duty be imposed to protect the industry and keep the Canadian market for Canadians.
I should like to discuss for a few moments the question of steel. It will be and is recognized by all-and I think this has particular application to Nova Scotia-that the industries of coal and steel are inter-dependent and interlocked. It cannot be denied by any hon, member that the steel industry in the Dominion of Canada has been sufficiently protected to enable it to survive and compete with other industries along the same lines. I read a few minutes ago in connection with the coal industry an extract from the report of the committee that waited on the government in 1924 requesting additional duties on coal. In the same report I find there are extracts in connection with the steel industry in Canada. Let me read some of them:
The steel industry of Nova Scotia is the only portion of the general steel industry of Canada which is in any real sense self-contained, or able to produce manufactured material of genuinely Canadian origin.
It is the one industry of iits kind in Canada the output of which is the result of the expenditure of practically its total cost in the form of wages paid to Canadian or other British workmen.
The coal used is mined by Canadians, the ore by Canadians assisted iby their neighbour Britishers in Newfoundland, while all the work of smelting and refining is done in Canada by Canadians, many of 14011-184
whom have given years to the acquisition of their art which is now a valuable asset that is in danger of being lost to their native country. In the other steel plants in Canada both coal and ore for making pig iron and refining it to steel are imported from the United States, and should that source of raw materials for any reason become unavailable, iron and steel manufacture and the fabrication of iron and steel into finished goods would necessarily cease.
For this reason the steel industry of Nova Scotia deserves especial consideration. It is the only possible native source of the primary material of the iron and steel arts, and for national preservation, and to avoid complete dependence upon the outside for iron and steel supplies, requires to be kept in existence.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am informed it is estimated that for the past seventeen years Canada has, in round figures, imported over 500,000 tons yearly of iron and steel in the form of pig iron, billets, plates, bars and rods, due wholly to inadequate protection, and in some instances to inequality of freight rates. Our steel importations from the United States alone now closely approach, if indeed they do not exceed, 2,000 tons per working day. Belgium is shipping iron rods into Canada at prices several dollars per ton below our cost of production. Meanwhile, our furnaces are cold and thousands of our men idle, with a certain percentage of our coal output uncalled for.
Our importations of iron and its products for the year ending February 1926 amounted to $171,165,943. Of this amount we imported from the United States alone over $150,000,000 worth. During the same period we exported to the United States $7,225,561 worth. That leaves a difference against us of over $145,000,000. During the same period we imported from the United Kingdom $17,638,2312 worth, and we exported to the United Kingdom about $8,000,000 worth. For the year ending February 1926 we imported from all countries iron and steel products to the value of $174,165,943, and we exported $72,855,942. In other words, there is a balance against us on iron an-d its products of over $100,000,000.
A short time ago, Mr. Ross H. McMaster, the president of one of our large steel industries in Canada, made the following statement in connection with the steel industry:
Steel manufacture is a basic industry in 'this as in other countries, but iit has been exposed in recent years to growing competition, facilitated by tariff reductions. An average duty of less than 10 per cent does not protect, the result being that steel imports have nearly equalled the domestic output, and that Canadian production has increased by less than one and one-half per cent in fifteen years, as against an increase of 75 per cent in the United States, the Canadian production for 1925 being actually lower the output in 1912.
The Budget-Mr. Smith

Mr. McMaster goes on to say:
Some in Canada will state that the profits of the Steel Company are large.
He refutes the assertion, and in the concluding paragraph states that they have earned a dividend rate of but 2^ per cent on the capital invested. That d-oes not appear to me to be a very exorbitant rate of interest for that or any other industry.
I am also reliably informed, Sir, that 51,600 tons of steel rails were imported in 1924. Had those rails been bought in Sydney, hundreds of men in the steel mills would have had three months more work, while the coal miners at Sydney would have had 115,000 more working days and $2,000,000 which left this country would have been kept here.

The steel industry has been crippled; the production has fallen below that of fifteen years ago; other countries of the world are absorbing our Canadian market; our manufacturers are losing the home market -all these indisputable facts call for a complete revision upward of the tariff on steel. Now I want to pass on to the textile industry. This is one of our most important industries; it employs 19 per cent of our total industrial workers; it pays 15 per cent of the total industrial wages; it produces 14 per cent of our total manufactured products and employs 9 per cent of the total industrial capital engaged. To show the magnitude of this industry-and I am sure this will be interesting to my western friends-within the past ten years there have been times when the value of the textile products manufactured in Canada was greater than the value of the wheat crop. In 1923 the value of our textile products amounted to the colossal sum of $334,439,196.

I would like to point out also that in the fiscal year 1925 Great Britain exported to Canada 82 per cent of the manufactures of wool coming to this country; the United States 6 per cent, and other countries 12 per cent. In the calendar year 1923, the latest I have showing both home production and imports, the total value of all manufactured woollen and knit goods imported into Canada amounted to $40,700,908, of which goods to the value of $33,111,173 came from Great Britain. In 1924 we imported from Great Britain 30,154,200 square yards of woollen and worsted cloth. English manufacturers of textiles are applying for protection in the Old Land; they ask for a 33J per cent ad valorem duty on foreign woollens and worsted cloth.
I pass from that phase of the subject, to return later. In the fiscal year 1925 the total imports from Great Britain amounted to $151,100,207, of which $72,128,723 represented textile produets. On examining the imports from Great Britain it will be immediately seen that approximately 50 per cent were in competition with our own textile industry, while the remaining 50 per cent is spread over all the other industries in Canada.
Now we come to the effect the French treaty has had in Canada, and I would like to classify it briefly as having two main effects. In the first place it increases the amount of goods made in France and sold in Canada; in the second place it replaces goods made by workers in Canadian mills. The increased imports of cloth from France under the French treaty and the increased importation from Great Britain are closing our mills, and to-day many of our Canadian workmen are out of work. It is an undeniable fact, I think, that a good many of our textile workers are without employment, and a great many of them have left for the United States, which amply protects its textile industry. In H011-1841
the town from which I come we have a very good example of the effect the tariff is having on the textile industry. An industry which in 1921 employed approximately 200 men today employs but two, a night watchman and a day watchman.

It has been mentioned before, but it is important and will bear repetition that in Canada we have only about 2,500,000 sheep, which is practically the number we had thirty or forty years ago; in other words, there has been no growth whatever in the sheep raising industry in this country. I am informed that we use in Canada annually 70,000,000 pounds of wool, and that our sheep supply only 15,000,000 pounds of our annual consumption. I realize the fact, whidh has been pointed out before, that Australia is particularly well adapted to the raising of sheep because they can graze there practically the whole year. This advantage is offset, however, by the fact that the sheep in Australia have to endure droughts, and are also subject to diseases to which our sheep in Canada are not susceptible. In 1897 a system of specially low duties on goods manufactured in Great Britain was granted by Canada and increased to one-third off the general tariff in 1900. Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to show the attitude displayed towards this very important industry in the United States by the president. He said:
I confess that I desire to see our country prosperous;
I am aware there can be no prosperity in which the textile industry does not have a generous share.
President Coolidge said at Washington, April 6:
There are sound and accepted historians who date the beginning of the modern phase of the industrial epoch from the invention of power-driven machinery for textile making.
From our national beginning it has been an almost uniform policy to conserve to the American producers the rights of first opportunity in the home market. The American home market is the most wonderful commercial development in all human experience.
The fact that our buying and consuming capacity is so great proves that, despite some inequities, we have on the whole maintained a more equitable distribution of the proceeds of industry than has been possible in less favoured communities. We are reaching a very fair approximation of democracy in industry.	_
Tiie pride of quality and craftsmanship has always been maintained to a notable degree throughout most of the textile industry. It necessarily denotes the payment of as liberal wages as the business can justify, and thereby the establishment of a great community of skilled and intelligent workers. Industrial prosperity depends almost entirely on men and women of skill.
The Budget-Mr. Smith

Industry has come thoroughly to recognize its responsibilities towards its employees. The government approves of and shares in that responsibility. It has come to be recognized almost universally that only upon justice to wage-earners of the nation can there be reared any lasting prosperity.
It seems to me that if we would adopt a similar motto in this country we would be doing something of a very substantial and commendable character toward this industry. I spoke a few minutes ago about an industry in the town of Amherst, which is in the constituency I represent. I have a letter from the president of the Stanfield concern which was located there-the buildings are still there but they are not in operation-in which he relates some matters of interest. In reference to the Amherst mills he states:
We found we were not getting a new dollar back for the old dollar expended; were wearing down our plant, and it was better to close down-take our liquid assets and convert them into cash and loan same out. The past twelve months have proved to us that this was a wise course for us to take in the interests of our shareholders.
He states further:
A beautiful mill like the Amherst Woollen Mills, if in the States, would be worth hundreds of thousands of dollars and would be employing hundreds of workmen. The same thing applies to a less extent to the Oxford Woollen Mills. *
He further states in his communication to me:
Years ago there were in the province of Nova Scotia woollen mills at Yarmouth, Eureka, Hopewell, Amherst, Oxford and Truro.
I think I am correct in saying that of all those mills referred to, the one at Truro is the only one in operation to-day. The Oxford Woollen Mills recently commenced operations on a small scale in the hope that they may be able to compete under the serious disadvantage to which they are subjected. I had a letter which I wished to read for the benefit of my hon. friends from Winnipeg in connection with the attitude of labour in the Dominion of Canada towards the textile industry. I am sorry I have mislaid it, but it was quite significant and stated in substance that the textile workers in the Dominion of Canada were not being treated fairly by the government in that their markets were being absorbed by foreign countries, and that if this policy of allowing other countries to come in and absorb the markets was continued they could not hope for anything of an encouraging nature for the workers in the textile industry of Canada.
I desire to speak for a few minutes on the question of the boot and shoe industry and its relation to the tariff, another matter that 
has been entirely overlooked by the Minister of Finance. The manufacture of boots and shoes is usually one of the first things to start in any country. Footwear is undoubtedly a necessity. There usually is a domestic supply of hides, so that one finds the primary condition for manufacturing, namely, a demand for the product and a supply of the raw material. This is another industry which, I submit, is suffering on account of unfair competition, and an industry for which there has been no relief under the tariff. This industry is one of the oldest in Canadian history. As far back as 1667, the Jesuits wrote to France that as a country could not be formed entirely without the assistance of manufactures, an industry was already in operation making shoes and hats and another was in contemplation for linen and leather. From its early beginnings the shoe industry has been completely revolutionized, and the manufacture of fine shoes in this country may be said to date from only about 18S5 or 1890. This development has been accomplished against tremendous odds and in the face of many handicaps. United States factories for a long time supplied a very large proportion of the fine footwear sold in the Dominion, our factories not being able to afford to manufacture those finer types and styles.
It may be interesting to note that during the war the shoe industry consolidated its position and proved to the world that its product in all lines was second to none. We made 3,000,000 pairs of army shoes during the conflict, and in the years 1919 and 1920 we exported to twenty-five countries, our exports of boots and shoes amounting in 1920 to $5,678,720. After the war other countries started to adjust their tariffs and Canada's export market was shut off, the result being that Canada's exports of boots and shoes for the twelve months ended February, 1926. amounted to only $265,000 as against $5,678,720 in 1920. The industry to-day is operating at approximately seventy-five per cent of its full time capacity.
It is significant that the production of boots and shoes in Canada last year was less than the output in 1912 by 1,800,000 pairs and, that while Unitecf States factories increased their production from 313,230,157 pairs in 1921 to 323,553.055 pairs in 1925, the Canadian output dropped from 15,800,000 pairs in 1924 to 15,500,000 pairs in 1925. It is estimated that more than a hundred shoe manufacturing firms have failed or been forced into financial reorganization since 1920. During the last four or five years the shoe factories have been operating at a loss.

Calvin E. Coolidge, President of the United States, said:
We have built agriculture squarely into the structure of our protective system, and the American farmer must not be undersold at 'home by New Zealand mutton, Argentine beef, Canadian wheat, Danish butter, Bulgarian tobacco, Chinese eggs or Cuban sugar.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that we have been following since 1922 a most mystifying and peculiarly absurd fiscal policy in this country. In the light, knowledge and complete understanding of what tariff measures practically the whole civilized world has adopted since the war affording more adequate protection, we in Canada stand as the only country of importance adopting a policy of an opposite character, namely the lowering of our tariff barriers.
That the question of trade is one of international niceties and fraught with intricacies, we all admit. That we must adhere to some extent to international trends, to hold our own in international trade relations with the world, is axiomatic. The world's policy is against us in our costly experiment. We are a strong, virile and intelligent people; our country is teeming in a wealth of natural resources, the envy of civilization. A great deal depends on our international attitude under the world's trading policy as to whether we will be able to forge ahead in the race for international trade supremacy. With our country's fiscal policy out of step with the world; with our markets held for andl being absorbed by foreign countries; with our industries shattered or stultified; with our exodus to highly protectionist countries, we should learn at least the simple lesson that, clever as we may be, proud and courageous as our government may wish to appear in the eyes of the world, we are as yet a small, struggling nation bent on building up our country. We should be following a main essential recognized world policy of protection that will inure to the safeguarding of our small and crippled industries; to keep our Canadians in Canada, to hold our Canadian markets for Canadians, and to protect all other interests. We fail in our purpose, in our obligations to the labouring classes, to our agricultural interests; to our industrial structure; we fail to promote our country's general welfare and to recognize our duty to posterity unless we pursue the course of recognized international advantage by safeguarding and protecting every legitimate interest in the Dominion of Canada.

May I also observe at this point that special trade agreements with individual nations are now so common as to have become the more popular means of encouraging international trade, and the present government has very wisely sought to break down international trade barriers by proceeding along these lines.
In addition to the substantial reductions which the Laurier government made in the tariff, it gave to this country a record of clean, efficient and progressive government, and, Sir, the brightest page in that fifteen years' record is the page which records the fact that that administration was asked to step down and out because its great leader staked its life on a question of high principle, without even a breath of scandal having been attached to its name. The fact that that administration was defeated fighting on the finest low tariff platform ever presented to the people of Canada is the pride of every Liberal, as it was the crowning satisfaction of our noble leader.
Following that record, we had a ten year term of Tory government in this country, of which the less said the better. Had it not been for the remarks of the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) yesterday, I would have let it go in silence, but, Sir, after fifteen years of progress such as this country attained under the Laurier ad-
]Mr. McMillan.]
ministration, and with only an increase in ordinary expenditure of some $4,000,000 per annum, their successors in the three years before the war increased the ordinary expenditure by over $36,500,000. They had become so extravagant that even their own political friends were saying freely that they were squandering the money of this country like a lot of drunken sailors.
Then came the war, and in its direction and prosecution, together with the debasement and desecration of the franchise through the medium of the War-time Elections Act and the Soldiers' Voting Act, both of which are the special children of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), we had the most diabolical government record of mismanagement and maladministration which ever stained the pages of Canadian history. In the face of such a record, and after the way they borrowed money and added to the national debt more than Canada's entire war cost and cost of demobilization, at a time when they could have and should have collected hundreds of millions of dollars in war time taxation-in the face of such a record, it is a wonder to me that hon. gentlemen opposite are not reticent, rather than charging this government with delaying the return of prosperity to this country.

The Budget-Mr. McMillan
As a result of the record of hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in power, no Canadian government ever assumed office under greater difficulties than the present King administration. Their first act was to bring order out of chaos. Their work of reconstruction was necessarily slow, and it had to be done with care. They had to face enormous annual expenditures of nearly $464,000,000, and they could only effect reform through lessened taxation and otherwise as their carefully planned gradually reducing expenditures would permit. But their record is good. In the four years time, without taking the National railways into account-I believe we should discuss the business of the National railways in this House, but I say again now, as I said in my remarks on January 21, that I believe we should keep the business of the Canadian National Railways separate from the general public business of this country-this government has been able in the four years to reduce the expenditure by $354,000,000 below the basis of the last year of the Meighen administration.
The very first act of this administration was a marvellous stroke of business for the Canadian people. In the appointment of Hon. P. C. Larkin as High Commissioner, this government obtained the services of a man of outstanding diplomatic and business ability. His record to date is one of which every Canadian may well be proud. While the Borden government had received the promise in 1917 that the cattle embargo would be removed, yet they sat on the fence until the Hon. Mr. Larkin went over there in 1922, and in eight months' time, on the 15th day of December, 1922, he was able to see the statute finally removing the emhargo obtain the royal assent.
Apart from the ordinary duties to which the office of High Commissioner had previously confined itself, Mr. Larkin has been able to collect for the Canadian government $136,313,795 from different countries. These were debts w'hich had been lying idle for three or four years before he went over, and our government was receiving neither principal nor interest on account of these debts. He has also succeeded in funding the $24,000,000 Roumanian loan and the $11,000,000 loan to Greece, on account of both of which we are now receiving interest, and sinking fund payments regularly. These were debts which Sir Vincent Meredith, president of the Bank of Montreal, had considered hopeless, but the high commissioner has been able to secure in those, obligations which are as good as gold.
Coming now to the budget proposals ami the reductions proposed in the tariff, I am
not surprised at the calamity howls that have been going up from across the way. Why, it would not be the Conservative party if they did not indulge in that kind of thing, and the very fact that they offer such a half-baked amendment to the budget shows to us that they are not sincere in what they are saying. I go further. I believe that we will get ninety per cent of the people to favour these budget proposals. What did the Conservative party do two years ago? Their howling was the same when this government reduced the agricultural implement duties They said the agricultural implement industry was going to be destroyed, and the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) even went so far the other day as to say that it had been destroyed, and that there were very few mowers and self-binders being manufactured in this country now, but that we were supplying our needs from the United States. What are the facts? For the fiscal year 1921-1922, 1,271 mowers came into this country from the United tSates; for the twelve months ending February, 1925, only 396 mowers came into Canada. For the twelve months ending in February of the present year, only 353 mowers came into this country. So that we have an importation of 353 mowers in the year ending February, 1926, as against 1,271 in the year 1921-22 when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power. When it comes to self-binders what do we find? For the fiscal year ending March, 1921, the imports of self-binders into Canada numbered 5,485. For the twelve months ending February, 1924, the number was 3,226, and for the year ending February, 1926, there was an importation of 2,118. But hon. gentlemen opposite told us nothing about the exports of agricultural implements from Canada to the United States. What do we find to be the case in this regard? In 1921-22 the export amounted to $583,005. For the twelve months ending in February. 1925, the figure had grown to $1,201,179, and for the twelve months ending February. 1926, it had increased still further to $2,324,073. These were exportations into the United States, meeting the competition of American manufacturers in their own country. Now let me take the total export of agricultural implements.

twelve months ending February, 1926, the total export amounted to $13,516,407, showing that the manufacturers of agricultural implements were thriving as they had never done before.
It will be the same in the case of the automobile industry. We hear very humiliating references to the manufacturers of automobiles; a reference of that kind was made last evening to Mr. Henry Ford. May I be permitted to say that Mr. Ford is the kind of manufacturer that we want to see in this country? We want here men who are willing to rely on their own resources rather than on government favours. I am surprised to observe how hon. gentlemen opposite endeavour to decry the standard of the Canadian people. We have the best people in the world, able to meet competition from any country. We farmers are ready and willing to do that, and I believe that if the matter were fairly placed before them the majority of the people of this country would support that stand. We hear quite a lot about automobiles these days, but in my opinion at no distant date there will be more automobiles sold than ever. The increased production will give employment to more workingmen, a greater number of men will be engaged in the trade, and the same satisfactory results will be noticeable in the case of that industry as in the case of the agricultural industry today.
Coming to the matter of electric light plants for the farmers, hon. gentlemen opposite have not much to say about it. If there is one class in the community that are entitled to the benefits of electric lighting plants in their homes where they cannot be served by the hydro it is the hard-working farmers of the country, and more especially the farmers' wives. The present government is entitled to the highest credit for reducing the duties on the machinery necessary for power and lighting purposes on the farm. What are the facts in that connection? There was formerly a thirty-five per cent duty, but when we required repair parts we had to pay fifty per cent over the American price list. It was time to make a reduction of duty in that direction. Oh, the poor farmer I Hon. gentlemen opposite have been shedding tears over the state of the poor Ontario farmer, and claiming credit for the manner in which they wish to come to his relief. The hon. member for South Wellington, in his speech the other day, declared that the farmers of Ontario were thoroughly protectionist in sentiment. He made that statement in the face of the fact that the six townships in his own rid-
]Mr. McMillan.]
ing turned him down by the handsome majority of 1,709 votes, the largest Liberal majority, I believe, that was ever accorded in the history of those townships. When I hear hon. gentlemen opposite express so much solicitude about the Ontario farmer, I am reminded of the many arguments that have been advanced in this House since 7th January, which depend so greatly upon the little word "if". Let me say that "if" hon. gentlemen opposite could only shed enough tears to float themselves on to the treasury benches, the floor of this chamber would become a lake in less time than is occupied in making this statement. WThen we hear hon. gentlemen opposite arguing that we should impose high duities upon agricultural products in order to benefit the Canadian farmer it reminds me of the words of Thomas Carlyle respecting the corn laws of England, when he said:
Impartial persons have to say with a sigh, that for bo long back they have heard no argument for it but such as might make the angels and almost the very jackasses weep.
The arguments of hon. gentlemen are on a par with this expression. Perhaps the present moment is an opportune time to refer to a statement made during the general election by the right hon. leader of the opposition. The statement in question was that when two hundred thousand people left this country they carried with them a purchasing power in agricultural products to the value of $100,000,000. What does this mean? It means that every man, woman and child carries with them a purchasing power of $500 per capita. According to the press reports this statement, or its equivalent, was made at Wing-ham, Chatham, Charlottetown and Calgary, showing that the right hon. gentleman wished to give it nation-wide publicity. What are the facts? As I have already shown, in 1923 the total agricultural production of Canada was $1,342,132,000, of which $543,601,734 was exported, leaving less than $800,000,000 to feed our live stock and support our 9,000,000 people, which is not $500 per capita but less than $90 per capita. Is it possible that the truth in this case was not sufficiently high sounding to suit the right hon. gentleman's purpose, and in order to make it so he was willing to stretch the figures to over five times their breaking point? In view of such expressions on the part of these public men is it any wonder if the farmers of Canada pause and hesitate, and ask themselves the question: Must we, or can we, put any degree of confidence in these would-be champions of the farmer's cause?

The Budget-Mr. McMillan
Now, Sir, take that same production and that same exportation, 1543,601,000 which is sent out to the markets of the world, where the price is set, and which regulates the price of the same articles at home. Knowing that, the most superficial observer ought to know it would make no difference to the price if the government put one hundred per cent duty on this class of products. You cannot through the medium of a high tariff increase the domestic price of any article of which there is a large exportable surplus. So that this whole talk about high tariff duties on farm products is a blind; and higher duties on small fruits and vegetables simply a lure to commit the Canadian farmer to sky-high protection for the benefit of another class. Small fruits and vegetables come in now under a 30 per cent duty. Is that not sufficient?

speechtext:
Does the hon.
gentleman not think the producers of these fruits and vegetables ought to be fairly good judges of what they want, and how is it they are passing resolutions and sending them in to the government asking for protection?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will deal with the
vegetables first. They only come into the country in any considerable quantity at a time when the Canadian farmers are not putting them on the market. In such a sectional matter as that involving small fruits and vegetables, or any other sectional matter, the interest of the great body of the people should always be the paramount consideration. Any government worthy of the name will always take a national rather than a parochial.point of view, and when it comes to the matter of vegetables we are shipping more vegetables to the United States by a considerable margin than they are shipping to us. For the twelve months ending February, 1926, our exports to the United States were as follows:
Potatoes (for 12 months ended Feb., 1926).. $3,968,893 Vegetables (.for 12 months ended Feb., 1926).	5,127,898
We imported from the United States $4,709,150 worth, so there is nothing to complain of in that. I say again that doubling the tariff duty on those articles which in the main do us no good will be used as a justification to double the duty on manufactured goods, and that will have the effect of increasing the price to the farmer himself and to the general consumer of this country.
Then my hon. friends talk about raising the duty. Have we heard one of them say in all their arguments that they desire higher duties on the goods which the manufacturer requires HOll-185
in his business? Not at all. In that respect they are absolute free traders, in that they want everything they require at the lowest possible price; but they are human, intensely human in that when it comes to their finished product they want to get the highest price they can, even to the extent of persuading the government to jack up the tariff to such a degree that like productions from other countries will not come in and as a consequence they will have the consumers of this country entirely to themselves. That is high protection such as this country will have if we ever allow hon. gentlemen opposite to take their seats on the treasury benches, but that is what we are going to prevent. Whenever a government begins to hand out special favours to any line of industrial activity through the medium of high tariff duties, they do an injustice to those who buy those goods; those people become dissatisfied and come to the government asking them to increase the duty on their finished products, and thus the vicious circle is begun and continued by one class of producers or manufacturers handing the increase on to the other. It goes all the way round the board until it comes back to the farmer, who cannot pass on his increased cost of production because the price of his goods is set in the markets of the world. So that it is a burden on the farmer which he cannot possibly remove, and it is also a burden on the working class consumer, who is required thereby to pay more than he ought to pay for every requirement on which high duties have been levied.
If there is one class in this country more than another to which the government should give special consideration, one class more than another to which they ought to be considerate, it is those God-fearing men and women who pledge themselves to each other for life, who establish homes, who raise families and bring them up to become the best citizens of the world. Such families are usually found upon the farm and among the middle and struggling classes of our people. To that great class a system of high protection is untrue. It places an unjust burden upon every home and family in the land in the unduly high prices they have to pay for every requirement upon which high duties are levied. Never was this fact more strongly impressed on me than on November 29, 1920, in London, Ontario, when I sat for hours while three members of the late Meighen government-sworn ministers of the crown, sworn servants of the people, sworn to do justice by all the people-sat fairly courting the evidence of men representing one manufac-



The Budget

Mr. McMillan
turing concern after another, as they came forward pleading for higher duties upon the goods they produced-and for what purpose? Simply to enable those manufacturers to put their hands a little deeper into the pockets of the people and take from them more than they ought to take for the goods they must buy.
That, Sir, is undoubtedly what high protection does, and assuredly what many producers will be allowed to do if the present Tory party are ever allowed to take their places upon the treasury benches of the government of this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What is the answer?
Mr. .McMILLAN: The answer is that economic conditions to-day are not at all what they were at that time. We have heard a great deal about foreign countries imposing high tariff duties and thus preventing us from trading with them and possibly I shall have something to say about that before I conclude.
Place me in a position whereby I can take a little toll from every individual in a community and I will rapidly become wealthy. It will take all the people in the community some little time to realize that my additional wealth is obtained at their cost, that they are being robbed for my benefit. That is precisely the way in which high protection acts, and if we ever allow these people to get on to the treasury benches of this country, that is what will occur. I say again: One class above all others to which a high protective tariff is unjust is the working classes and the farmers, so that the Liberal party are fighting the cause of the common people as against the encroachments of the specially privileged interests, fighting the battle of the struggling fathers and mothers who are busily engaged in providing their families with the necessary ]Mr. McMillan.]
food and raiment which ought to be given to them at the lowest possible price, and which, if this government continues to remain in power, will be given to them at the lowest possible price consistent with the revenue requirements of this country.
I have often heard it said that high tariff duties will give the artisans, the mechanics and the working classes better wages. Such is not the case; it is not borne out by the facts. I am not going to put the statements on Hansard again, but if bon. members will turn to page 329 of Hansard of the present-year they will find out what the heads of labour organizations and the president of the textile trade in the United States tell us regarding conditions in the textile trades in that country of high tariffs. We are also told that we ought not to encourage the importation of foreign manufactured goods; that we should produce at home everything which can be produced at home and so to such a degree discourage international trade. No greater mistake could be made by any Canadian government.
I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and the debate adjourned.
